newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ business confidence slips, still positive - bank.
newsitem.headline: NZ business confidence slips, still positive - bank.

text.p: New Zealand business confidence fell considerably in October but remains positive, the National Bank of New Zealand said on Thursday.
A NBNZ survey showed a net 12 percent of respondents now anticipate improved conditions in the year ahead, down from a net 21 percent in September.
However, the bank noted all of October's responses were received ahead of the general election on October 12.

"General elections tend to consume the business community's interest. The 1996 election was no exception. After heralding spring optimism last month, responses were less rosy this month," chief economist Adrian Orr said.
He said political limbo may continue to dampen confidence, as little new is known about the make-up of New Zealand's next government. Coalition negotiations are continuing.
Overall, however, the October results were encouraging, for although business confidence had baulked at the election hurdle, investment and employment prospects had improved.

"Of some concern is the nature of this confidence, being partly hinged on expected interest rate declines. These remain subject to any political shenanigans and plans for a rapid fiscal expansion," Orr said.

The New Zealand First party holds the balance of power after the inconclusive election, and is holding coalition talks with both the ruling conservative National Party and the left-of-centre Labour Party.
Orr said aside from election jitters, economic news had tended to be positive. The sharemarket remained buoyant, long term interest rates fell and June quarter GDP confirmed modest growth.

A net 28 percent of respondents in October expected interest rate declines, from a net 42 percent in September. Orr said that was despite the RBNZ's September economic projections, which implied no immediate rate relief.

Respondents' outlook for their own activity was marginally down, largely reflecting weaker confidence in the agriculture sector. Profit outlooks were still positive but down on last month, with the retail and construction sectors registering the largest falls.

Investment intentions improved for the fourth month in a row, with a net 17 percent of respondents anticipating a boost in investment over the coming year, led by the service, manufacturing and retail sectors.
Orr said construction intentions remained the wild card.

"Residential construction intentions have dragged themselves back into a net positive position from their July depths. The scent of lower interest rates is alluring," he said, adding that optimism nonetheless remained well short of the 1994 heydays.
The commercial construction sector faltered slightly in activity expectations.
